items.question: How do you assess the promise of Grover's algorithm for practical quantum optimization?
items.object: Grover's algorithm and practical quantum advantages for optimization
items.answer: Eventually, if you have a full, scalable quantum computer with error correction, we do know of algorithms that would give you modest advantages for these types of problems. In particular, there was a famous quantum algorithm called Grover's algorithm, discovered in 1996, and it basically lets you solve just about any search problem in roughly the square root of the number of steps that a classical computer would need, getting a quadratic speed-up. That could be a big deal, but that's not an exponential speed-up. If I had 10 to the thousand power possibilities to search through, the square root is 10 to the 500, still a quite big number. That could eventually push forward the frontier of what sizes of problems we could handle. But it will be a long time before any Grover-type speed-ups are actually a net win in practice, after you factor in all of the expense and all of the slowdown that comes from needing to run an error-corrected quantum computer in the first place.

items.question: Where do you have confidence that quantum computing can deliver exponential speed-ups?
items.object: Code breaking and quantum simulation as applications of quantum computing
items.answer:
There are quantum algorithms that get exponential speed-ups over anything we know how to do classically, but most are for two specific categories of problems. One of them is breaking cryptographic code. This was the famous application that put quantum computing on the map in the first place 30 years ago: Shor's factoring algorithm factors large numbers exponentially faster than any known classical algorithm, and its variants could break most of the public-key encryption that currently protects the internet. That would be a big deal.

The other is quantum simulation. If you're trying to design better batteries or better solar cells, you can simulate the dynamics of all the interacting electrons, even though the wave function is this enormous object and has a number of parameters that grows exponentially with the number of particles. A quantum computer would be the purpose-built device for handling that because it itself would have the same exponentiality. Those are the two big applications where we're quite confident that you could get an exponential speed-up: code breaking and quantum simulation.

items.question: How do you think people should assess quantum computing startups promising breakthroughs in optimization, AI, machine learning, and finance?
items.object: Quantum computing startups claiming advantages in optimization, AI, machine learning, and finance
items.answer:
Beyond the research aspect, I was talking to a guy at a company—he's talking about optimizing financial models—and I just lost him. I wince here, because there are possibly hundreds of startups right now that are about using quantum computing for optimization, especially machine learning and finance. I think that, at least as things stand right now, this is almost all phony.

That's mostly been the reason for this rush of venture capital and money for startup companies over the last decade: this narrative that quantum computers are going to revolutionize optimization, AI, machine learning, and finance. A lot of that is based on what I would consider a foundation of sand. It's based on quantum algorithms that are heuristic, which means none of us can really analyze or prove much of anything about their performance. If no one can prove that they won't give an exponential speed-up, people in the business world feel free to make the most optimistic assumption imaginable and say, “Let's just assume that this will get an exponential speed-up.” They learned about 15 years ago that when you say the word quantum, people's brains shut down. They think it's magic and they're ready to believe anything.

What I would encourage people looking at quantum computing startups to do: the number one question to ask that people don't ask is, does it beat a classical computer in a fair comparison? Don't tie the classical computer's hands behind its back by using some stupid algorithm; don't rig the comparison. Look at the best you could do with classical heuristic algorithms, such as simulated annealing, and compare that against the results from the quantum heuristic algorithm. Is there an advantage? If so, do we expect that advantage to widen as you go to larger and larger problems? Is there any empirical or theoretical reason why you expect better scaling behavior?

items.question: How do you understand the role of a quantum computer when someone says they're using one to solve an optimization problem?
items.object: The role of quantum computers in solving optimization problems
items.answer:
I haven't, for the most part, looked into the exact details. Any time someone says they're using a quantum computer for such and such, you have to think of the quantum computer as this special-purpose accelerator that's only used for one little subpart of the whole problem. No one uses a quantum computer to do the user interface or the compiler or the programming language. We have all these layers in our abstraction stack where, of course, we use classical computers because they're perfectly adequate.

What people really mean is that you're feeding a classical computer your optimization problem. You have a classical algorithm breaking it up into little pieces, and then it is trying to find pieces that are small enough that it can feed them to the quantum computer and get back answers to those subproblems that then have to be further processed classically. That's fine, as far as it goes.

items.question: How do you assess the quantum-computing industry's progress since D-Wave's early systems?
items.object: Progress in the quantum-computing industry since D-Wave's early systems
items.answer:
D-Wave were the earliest ones who realized, “We can just build systems with hundreds or thousands of qubits, and if we do that, people will be excited,” and they're not even going to demand to know how good these qubits are, how long they maintain their quantum state, whether it's actually good enough that I could get any benefit over a classical computer. In a sense they were pioneers, realizing that people just didn't care that much about the reality of whether you are beating a classical computer.

Since then, there are hundreds of companies of every possible level of seriousness, from companies that have some of the best scientists working on this, who I really hope succeed, all the way to complete frauds who are just sprinkling the word quantum onto things that have nothing to do with quantum computing. In particular, you now have a bunch of companies that can make qubits of enormously higher quality than D-Wave's. D-Wave had superconducting qubits that maybe maintained their quantum state for a matter of nanoseconds, and now the table stakes would be some tens of microseconds. If you look at what Google or IBM or Rigetti can do, it's a much smaller number of superconducting qubits, but the thing I care about is that they're of much higher quality. It's still not good enough to get a practical benefit over a classical computer, but it is getting there. Instead of being four or five orders of magnitude away in terms of the error rate, now maybe it's only one order of magnitude away. That is a genuine cause for excitement. Meanwhile, there's been corresponding progress in the other architectures: trapped ions, photonics, neutral atoms.

items.question: How do you distinguish the role of probability in quantum measurement from the way an isolated quantum system changes over time?
items.object: Measurement and deterministic evolution in quantum mechanics
items.answer: The basic way that a quantum state can change over time: there are two ways. One is measurement, and the other one is unitary transformation. Measurement is when I look, and that's the only part of quantum mechanics where probability enters the picture. When I make a measurement, I can force my quantum state to collapse, and it makes a choice probabilistically. That's actually the one place where probability ever enters in any known fundamental physics. But if I leave a quantum system isolated from its environment, then it's changing over time in a way that's completely deterministic.

items.question: How do you understand the engineering task of building a quantum computer?
items.object: The engineering task of building a quantum computer
items.answer:
I think of unitary transformations as rotations or reflections, but not in our three-dimensional space—in this enormously high-dimensional space, two to the 100 power or whatever, depending on how many qubits I have. The engineering goal in building a quantum computer is to do not just any unitary transformations on your qubits, but the specific unitary transformations that you want, which will cause the vector of amplitudes to evolve in a particular way that solves your computational problem.

In a classical computer, we're also trying to build up extremely complicated operations, like running the video software for a podcast or anything like that. Inside the microchip it's all ultimately broken down into Boolean logic gates, very simple operations that act on only one or two bits at a time. The most famous Boolean logic gates are AND, OR, and NOT. A very important theorem in Boolean logic says that if you string together enough AND, OR, and NOT gates, then you can express any Boolean function of any number of bits. Those simple operations are already universal; then it's just a question of how many you need and in what order you should apply them.

I'm telling you this because in quantum computing the story is closely analogous. Our goal with our quantum computer is to do some giant unitary transformation on all our qubits, like all thousand or million of them. To make that practical, we're going to break up the unitary transformation into a product of little tiny unitary transformations, each of which acts on only one or two of the qubits at a time. These are called quantum gates, the building blocks of any quantum computation.

items.question: How do you understand the division of work between a quantum algorithm designer and a quantum hardware engineer?
items.object: The division of work between quantum algorithm design and quantum hardware engineering
items.answer: In quantum algorithm design, I'm thinking: here is my collection of qubits, here are my allowed gates, and which gates do I apply to which qubits when? We have a notation for this called quantum circuit notation. It looks almost like a musical score: each qubit is a line going from left to right, and the gates are like different musical notes that we write down over those lines. Once they've written the quantum circuit, the quantum algorithm designer's job, or the quantum programmer's job, is done. Now the quantum hardware engineer's job begins. They need to take this sequence of gates and translate it into actual pulses that will act on these physical qubits in a way that has the effect of doing these gates.

items.question: How do you understand the hardware engineer's task of implementing quantum gates in a trapped-ion quantum computer?
items.object: Implementing quantum gates in trapped-ion quantum computers
items.answer:

They grab onto a nucleus with a laser and move it around. When two nuclei get close to each other, they have a natural electromagnetic interaction that causes some two-qubit unitary transformation. As I see it, the hardware person's job is just to shape that natural unitary into something that looks like a CNOT gate or whatever was the gate the quantum algorithm designer asked for.

items.question: How do you understand measurement as an engineering problem in quantum computing?
items.object: Measurement in quantum computing
items.answer: By measurement, I basically mean you have to take your spin state and it has to get recorded in something macroscopic. Typically, measurement devices work by an amplification effect: you'll have a single photon that deflects in a different way depending on whether this nucleus is spinning clockwise or counterclockwise. Then that photon could trigger a cascade of additional photons, and ultimately you have a whole photodetector array and it becomes something that's macroscopically detectable. You have to be very careful to only make the measurements when you're ready to. In some sense, a large part of the engineering problem of building a quantum computer is to prevent the environment from measuring your qubits before they're ready to be measured.

items.question: Why do you regard two-qubit gate fidelity as a more important measure of quantum computing progress than the number of qubits?
items.object: Two-qubit gate fidelity as a measure of quantum computing progress
items.answer:
You can't just ask about how many qubits. You have to ask what can you do with these qubits? How good are they? D-Wave will tell you, “Oh yeah, we have thousands of qubits, as many thousands as you want,” but they're trusting that people are not going to ask, “Can I actually beat a classical computer with them?” At any rate, that was D-Wave a decade ago. I've heard that they've become more cautious since then.

For me, the single most important number to look at is actually the two-qubit gate fidelity, which means with what degree of accuracy can I apply a single two-qubit entangling gate of my choice? When I entered the field 20 or 25 years ago, it would have been spectacular if you could do a single two-qubit gate with 50% fidelity. A decade ago it became 90% fidelity, then 95%. Some people have scaled up even to hundreds of qubits—I think IBM has—but not with fidelity that's quite that good.

items.question: How do you understand quantum error correction's significance for the feasibility of scalable quantum computers?
items.object: Quantum error correction and the threshold for scalable quantum computing
items.answer:
To help orient people on where we are: the key discovery in the mid-'90s that made people feel that building a quantum computer is merely a staggeringly hard engineering problem, and doesn't require any new fundamental physics, was the discovery of quantum error correction. In order to build a reliable quantum computer with as many qubits and gates as you want, you don't have to get the error all the way down to zero. That was the fear, because if you had to get error all the way down to zero, that's never going to happen; it's unrealistic. What people discovered in the '90s was that you only have to get the error down to some very low, nonzero level, and clever quantum generalizations of error-correcting codes can take care of the rest and push your effective or encoded error rate all the way down to zero.

The original estimate from 1996 was that you needed 99.9999% fidelity of two-qubit gates, basically that you could tolerate a one-in-a-million chance of error. That seemed ridiculously far from where anyone was technologically, but it at least proved the principle that there's only a finite amount of engineering that has to be done, not an infinite amount. With the more recent error-correcting codes that people have developed, it looks like you could build a scalable quantum computer if you have two-qubit gates with 99.99% fidelity—four nines. If you remember where I told you we are right now, I think the experimentalists are closing in on 99.9% fidelity, three nines. If you plot that on a graph, it looks pretty on track. If this effort continues, we should eventually get to the threshold where error correction becomes a net win. Once you've crossed that threshold, how many qubits you want is just a question of cost, like with a classical computer. If you want two million qubits instead of one million, that's more engineering, but you've figured out how to keep your qubits alive for as long as you need them, and there's no fundamental limitation on how many more you can add.

items.question: Why did you pursue boson sampling as a way to demonstrate quantum supremacy with a quantum computer that lacked error correction?
items.object: Quantum supremacy demonstrations and boson sampling
items.answer:
That came out of work that my student and I did in 2011, where we said, “People are talking about what can you do that's useful with a non-error-corrected quantum computer, but maybe we should first try to pin down: can you do anything at all that is classically hard, even if it's not useful?” We came up with a proposal for how you might do that, which was called boson sampling, adapted to optical quantum computing. The optics people got very interested and started doing small-scale experiments with five or six photons. At that point it's still trivial for a classical computer to simulate.

Let's just do a quantum supremacy demonstration,” with, I think, 60 or 70 qubits. This wouldn't exactly be boson sampling because their hardware was not designed for it, but they said, “Let's do something like boson sampling, adapted to our hardware.” We talked to them at the time and helped them figure out what that experiment would be. We adapted the theory of boson sampling to the kind of hardware that they had.

items.question: How do you assess the computational advantage demonstrated by Google's 2019 quantum supremacy experiment?
items.object: Google's 2019 quantum supremacy experiment
items.answer: In 2019 they announced results with 53 qubits, about 20 layers of gates, about a thousand gates, and they solved this sampling task. At the time they estimated that it might take 10,000 years for a classical computer to do the same thing, and that number got quoted all over the press. I think you have to be really careful with these numbers, because the classical computer scientists came along and said, “No, we can spoof this a lot faster with a classical computer.” If you're willing to spend enough money to have enough parallel classical processors, you can simulate the Google experiment faster than the experiment itself. It all comes down to energy and money. By those metrics, on these quantum supremacy benchmarks, the quantum computers are still winning, but only by a couple of orders of magnitude, not by a whole lot. There's an urgent need for better quantum supremacy experiments that will reestablish a clear speed-up.

items.question: How do you assess the prospects for useful noisy intermediate-scale quantum computing before error correction?
items.object: The prospects for useful noisy intermediate-scale quantum computing before error correction
items.answer: By analogy, before the transistor was invented, we had only much noisier building blocks for classical computers, like vacuum tubes or electromechanical relays, but those still worked well enough for people to do various useful things with them, among which was winning World War II. You could hope that maybe the same will happen here: even before we get truly error-corrected qubits, we'll have qubits that last just long enough that we can eke out some advantage. If we're going to do that, the best hope by far is that we'll do that for some sorts of quantum simulation problems, such as simulating the properties of various materials. There's a much better hope of doing something scientifically interesting and new and classically hard than there is of also doing something commercially useful, which is a higher bar to clear. People are working on that. The point is, there is no guarantee. Nature will have to be kind to us for us to get clear quantum computing speed-ups before error correction. After error correction, we're much more confident that we could get such speed-ups.

items.question: How do you understand the role of theory in the machine-learning progress that produced GPT-3?

items.question: How do you understand the mechanism of watermarking text generated by a language model such as GPT?
items.object: Watermarking language-model output
items.answer:
This is where we slightly change the way that our language model, such as GPT, operates. Language models are inherently probabilistic. You have this transformer neural network that's always taking as input the context of the previous however many words, and then it's generating a probability distribution over the next word. In normal operation, we sample according to that distribution. Sometimes the distribution will be very centered on one possibility, like if I say “the ball rolls down the,” then GPT is nearly certain that the next word is “hill.” In other cases, it's balanced between several possibilities, or even dozens of them.

With watermarking, we choose the next word, the next token, in a way that is secretly deterministic but looks random. It looks like we're doing it according to the distribution GPT said to sample from; a casual user can't tell the difference at all. But we're actually choosing the next word deterministically in a way that biases a score we can calculate later, given only the text. We're doing it in a way that systematically favors certain combinations of words.

items.question: How do you think about the safety tradeoff in open-sourcing generative AI models?

Once the model is open source, people can do what they want with it. That's true not just for watermarking, but for pretty much any safety mitigation you could possibly think of. Empirically, if you fine-tune your model by RLHF, reinforcement learning with human feedback, to only give safe, helpful, inoffensive answers, it takes about two days for people to take an open-source model and remove that fine-tuning. Then the model will spout whatever racist invective or bomb-making instructions you want it to.

That's the tradeoff with open-sourcing models, and I think it fundamentally depends on how powerful the model is. Stuff at the level of GPT-2 has already been open-sourced. Stuff at the level of GPT-3 probably is in the process, or soon will be. GPT-4, I feel that OpenAI made a very defensible decision not to open-source. Aside from the obvious commercial reasons why OpenAI doesn't want to open-source it, I do think there's also a safety issue there. Eventually you may get AIs powerful enough that open-sourcing them is kind of like open-sourcing thermonuclear weapons.

items.question: How do you assess the prospects for quantum computers to become broadly useful for AI?
items.object: Practical quantum speedups for AI and machine learning
items.answer:
I think those are indeed enormous questions. A large part of the question of how useful a quantum computer will be is tied up with how useful it will be for those tasks. But we're up against a fundamental difficulty that goes all the way back to the beginning of quantum algorithms, say 30 years ago, which is that if you want an exponential speedup from a quantum computer, it seems to be only for very specialized problems that we can get them. The two really huge examples where we're pretty confident that a quantum computer could give us an exponential speedup are simulating quantum mechanics itself and breaking public-key cryptography that currently protects the internet.

What people usually want to do in AI falls into neither of those two categories. You're given some arbitrary system of constraints and want to satisfy as many as possible, or you're given a loss function and want to set the weights in your neural network to minimize your loss function. For those types of tasks, we do know a quantum algorithm that can generically help. It's called Grover's algorithm. Grover's algorithm can take any list of n possible solutions to some problem and find a good solution, if there is one, in only about the square root of n steps. You should think of n, the number of possible solutions, as something truly enormous. You could easily have, in a combinatorial problem, two to the thousand power possible solutions. What's the square root of two to the thousand? It's two to the 500. That's a smaller number, but still quite enormous. That's the kind of speedup Grover's algorithm can give you, and for many tasks in AI and machine learning, almost 30 years later, that's still the most that we would know how to do even with a perfectly functioning quantum computer.

There's even a further difficulty, which is that to run a quantum computer at all, and actually run it at scale with thousands or millions of qubits, we expect that you would need something called error correction to get the qubits to work reliably. Error correction imposes an overhead. It might mean that you need thousands of physical qubits to simulate just a single qubit of your algorithm, a single logical qubit as we call it. If we're talking about Shor's factoring algorithm, which gets an exponential speedup, then that exponential speedup can still win out over a factor of a million slowdown. With Grover's algorithm, if you're paying a factor of a million overhead and the speedup you're getting is only square root, then the crossover point where that starts outperforming what you could do with a classical computer gets pushed out even further into the future. In order for the Grover speedup to be practical, which is really when I think quantum computers would start being broadly useful for AI, either you need super enormous quantum computers or someone has to discover a better way of doing error correction with a lower overhead.

items.question: How did Ewin Tang's work change your assessment of the proposed quantum speedup for recommendation systems?
items.object: Quantum recommendation algorithms and Ewin Tang's dequantization result
items.answer:
There was a clear claim to get a quantum speedup for recommendation systems, like the kind of thing Netflix does, recommending movies to users. That was proposed in 2016, and I really liked it because I could see that it got around all of these issues. I gave a student who was actually an 18-year-old undergrad at UT Austin, Ewin Tang, the problem: can you prove that this quantum speedup is for real? Prove that any classical algorithm that gives you the same information about the user's preferences would take exponentially longer than the quantum algorithm.

My student Ewin spent a year on that problem, and after a year of failed attempts came to me and said, "Listen, I think the reason I haven't been able to prove this is that it's not true. I think there is a classical algorithm that's only polynomially slower than the quantum algorithm." I was skeptical, but I told her to pursue this, and it turned out to be right. That was a breakthrough result about five years ago, which destroyed one of the main examples we had of how you might get an exponential quantum speedup for machine learning problems. Building on Ewin's breakthrough, a whole bunch of other quantum machine learning algorithms have now been dequantized, or as I like to say, Ewin-ed.

items.question: What makes quantum machine learning scientifically interesting to you despite the uncertainty about its practical advantages?
items.object: Quantum machine learning as a scientific research field
items.answer:
I still think quantum machine learning is extremely interesting as a scientific subject. We ought to know what the limits are here: can we figure out some killer app for quantum computers in machine learning problems, or if we can't, then why not? That's something I equally want to know.

Of course, there are lots of machine learning problems that themselves involve quantum mechanics, where you're trying to learn properties of a quantum state or properties of a Hamiltonian, which is the way that quantum states change over time. For those kinds of problems, it's a completely different story: yes, I'm very optimistic that quantum computers will help us a lot, and tools from quantum information will be relevant to understanding those problems. There's been a lot of progress there. Some of those are things I've worked on personally.

I've worked on procedures for learning properties of quantum states using exponentially fewer measurements than a naive approach would need. If you want to learn a full description of a quantum state of 100 qubits, there are two to the hundredth power parameters that you have to learn. That's an absolutely enormous learning problem. I had a paper in 2007 where I said, if we change the question a little and say you just need to predict the outcomes of most measurements on the state for some given probability distribution over measurements that have yes or no outcomes, then the amount of data that you need is exponentially smaller. It's only linear in 100; it's on the order of 100 data points that you need. The way I was able to prove that was by using techniques from classical machine learning, from classical computational learning theory, and combining those with quantum information theory.

Since then I've done many other things along the same line. One was called shadow tomography, about five years ago. I proposed a way that you could learn the outcomes of all measurements on your state that belong to some predetermined list, even if that list is very enormous. You can learn the outcomes of exponentially many different measurements on a state with exponentially many parameters by carefully measuring only a polynomial number of copies of the state. That again uses techniques from machine learning. There are lots of points of intersection between quantum computing and machine learning, whether or not quantum computers will be revolutionary for solving classical machine learning problems, which I regard as still very much an open question.

items.question: Why were you skeptical of arguments that researchers should drop their existing work to focus on preventing a superintelligent AI takeover?
items.object: Arguments that researchers should prioritize preventing a superintelligent AI takeover
items.answer:
I've been familiar with these arguments for a long time. I've known Eliezer Yudkowsky since around 2006, the sort of AI doom people who have been extremely worried about this particular scenario where AI becomes superintelligent and takes over. They've basically felt that everyone else should drop what they're doing and just think about that, and I was always very skeptical of that.

Partly, I felt like, even supposing that I agreed this was a big issue, who knows how long it will take for AI to reach a human or superhuman level? It could be hundreds or even thousands of years, for all we know. But supposing that were to happen in the next 20 years or whatever, what do you want me to do about it? I didn't see a research program there that had either math, like axioms that we all agree on and that we can prove theorems about, or experiments that we can do that tell us something useful. It all seemed like armchair philosophizing, imagining a super-powerful superintelligence that is almost godlike and can do whatever it wants, and almost anything it might want would be unaligned with human values, and then very quickly it just kills all humans, like The Terminator, The Matrix, or whatever, and takes over the world.

It was a very depressing subject because you just convince yourself over and over again that there is nothing you can do faced with such a superintelligence. You refute 10,000 ideas for things you could do by saying, "Okay, no, but the superintelligence will be too smart, and whatever strategy you have it will have foreseen it and found the way around that." It just didn't seem that there was that much meat. In quantum computing, we don't have a superintelligent AI and we don't have a scalable quantum computer either, but the difference is that with the quantum computer we can do all of this interesting math. We know exactly what the device should be, and we can start understanding what it will and won't be capable of. There are also the people who do experiments and are trying to build the actual machines, which seemed to me like actually an easy problem compared to replicating the human brain, compared to building an AI.

items.question: How have the achievements of GPT and DALL-E affected your thinking about AI?
items.object: GPT, DALL-E, and the empirical success of scaling neural networks
items.answer:
AI is changing the world. There are now artifacts like GPT and DALL-E that are way beyond where I would have expected AI to be by now. I didn't know that just taking neural networks and backpropagation, taking ideas that were around in the '80s, around when I was a student in the '90s, and scaling them up would produce such astounding results. Again, there are no theorems that tell us any of this stuff. The only test of all these things has been empirical.

I didn't predict these things; my only defense is that hardly anyone else predicted them either, including AI experts and even many of the ones who were most optimistic. They didn't know this particular approach was going to get as far as it would, but it has, and given that it's happened, the least I can do is update on that. I don't want to be like colleagues in computer science who look at what has happened in the past few years with GPT and other large language models, and whose main problem is inventing reasons why none of it counts, why none of this is true intelligence or impressive or interesting. It clearly is impressive, regardless of how we talk about what's going on inside these deep nets. I think they're clearly going to change the world at least as much as the internet did. That's just a loose lower bound at this point.

Of course I was very excited about that, but I didn't really know if there was anything a theoretical computer scientist like me could contribute. It's much harder to apply theory to AI than to quantum computing or cryptography, because of the issue we were talking about: the fact that AI works by exploiting real-world regularities that tend to be very hard to formalize.

items.question: How do you think about the value of watermarking AI-generated text when people can find ways to evade it?
items.object: Watermarking AI-generated text as a defense against misuse
items.answer: It is a cat and mouse game. Ultimately, even someone who just asks GPT to write their term paper in French and then puts it into Google Translate and fixes the errors, that would be a little bit more effort, but I don't know how to watermark text in a way that would survive translation from one language to another. There are other attacks one can think of. We can at least make it a little bit more expensive for people to use GPT in these ways and get started. Sometimes in a cat and mouse game there's nothing to do except try to be the best cat you can be. Google, I think, never discovered a principled solution to people trying to game search engine results, all the SEO people, but they just try to stay one step ahead of them. I could easily foresee the same thing happening with people using language models for academic cheating, propaganda, fraud, or all these different things.

items.question: How do you assess the prospects for making concrete technical progress in AI safety and alignment?
items.object: AI safety and alignment as technical research fields
items.answer:
I have other, more speculative, more theoretical projects, but it's been amusing for me that I would have weekly calls with Ilya, an extremely interesting and thoughtful guy. I would tell him about progress on watermarking and he would say, "Okay, that's great, Scott, you should keep thinking about that, but what we really want to know is how can you use computational complexity theory to define what it means for the AI to love humanity, and how can you define the concept of goodness in formal mathematical terms?" I'll keep thinking about that. Those are tough questions, harder to make progress on.

Of course, the reason why I decided to get involved this year is that now there are meaty problems where you can make clear progress. I don't feel like I have solved the watermarking problem, but I feel like I at least made an advance on it. One could work just on that watermarking problem for 10 more years and there would still be more to say about it. I feel like we're just in the very early days now of AI safety, AI alignment as a technical field where you can make actual legible progress.

items.question: Why do you find coherent extrapolated volition an interesting way to define the values an AI should have?
items.object: Coherent extrapolated volition as an approach to AI alignment
items.answer:
I have not succeeded in defining what it means for AI to love humanity. I think there actually are some interesting ideas that the AI alignment community has come up with about how to formalize these concepts. One that I like is something called coherent extrapolated volition. Basically, you don't want to train your AI on current human values, because what if we trained an AI on the human values of the year 1800 and it were to lock those in forever? That would be terrible. People believed terrible things in the year 1800, or at least things that we now almost universally regard as having been terrible. Surely today we also have values that, if we have descendants, they'll look back on with horror. We might be able to guess at what some of those are; we don't know for certain.

But what, in some sense, are the values that we want the AI to have? The values that we would have if we had 10,000 years to sit and think about it, if we could sit like the philosophers in Athens with our togas for thousands of years and debate and refine our moral intuitions, whatever views we would eventually come to. That might already be enough for the AI to go on. You might be able to tell an AI to simulate humans having this moral discussion for an enormous amount of time, which thousands of years might not actually be that much if you're an AI to simulate, and then implement whatever values humans would agree on after that much reflection. There are ideas like that. It's very hard to say anything mathematical and nontrivial about any of these proposals. I don't know that I've made much progress there.

items.question: Why do you think cryptographic backdoors could help make powerful AI models safe to shut down?
items.object: Cryptographic backdoors as off switches for powerful AI models
items.answer:
One question where I feel like maybe I did have something a little bit interesting was the question of an off switch. An off switch is the first AI alignment idea in the world, the first and most basic of either switching it off when it starts to go berserk or pulling the plug or whatever. The alignment people have for a long time had arguments that that's not good enough. Why isn't it good enough? Because if the AI is intelligent enough, it will have foreseen that the humans might turn it off, and it will probably have goals that would best be served if it's not switched off. Whatever its goals are, it can best pursue those goals if it's still on. It may have come up with a plan either to disable its off switch, talk the humans out of turning it off, or make copies of itself all over the internet. There's a whole subfield of AI safety called corrigibility, about how can you change the AI's objective if you decide it wasn't the right one, or as one special case, how can you switch it off.

What I realized is that there's been recent, really exciting work at the intersection of cryptography and machine learning that has shown, at least in some cases, how to insert a cryptographic backdoor into a machine learning model. There was a paper by Shafi Goldwasser, Vinod Vaikuntanathan, and two others. These are cryptographers; some of them are my former colleagues at MIT. For a certain depth of neural networks, they show that you can insert a backdoor where if the network gets this certain bizarre input, then it does some special thing that you want it to do, such as switching itself off. Even if you could see all the weights of the neural net, it would be computationally intractable for you to find that secret input if you weren't told it. You would have to solve a hard cryptographic problem. In that case, it's something called the planted clique problem: given a large graph that looks kind of random, find some anomalously large set of vertices that are all connected to one another. That's what is known in theoretical computer science as the planted clique problem, and they could show that finding the backdoor is at least as hard as solving that.

They viewed that mostly as a negative for AI safety: a bad person could insert this backdoor into a machine learning model that people would then use, and no one would be able to detect it, and that bad person could trigger the backdoor whenever they wanted to. Like many things in science, if the world gives you a lemon, you can make lemonade. Whether something is good or bad all depends on who is doing it. This could also be seen as a positive for AI alignment. What if we use these backdoors to insert a cryptographic off switch into a powerful AI model? You could have a robot where only humans know this secret instruction that will cause the robot to shut down, and even if the robot knows its own weights and could modify them, it would not easily find that shutdown instruction. That's an idea I've been playing with.

I think we're really at the beginning of this thing. I could easily imagine this being a large part of the whole future of cryptography: what kind of cryptographic stuff can you insert into a machine learning model, or how hard is it to detect that stuff once inserted? I've taken to calling this neurocryptography. Someone else suggested calling it deep crypto, but I'm not sure; I think we have to veto that name. That's something I've been thinking about. In some sense, I think it's possible to make progress here just because you don't really have to understand what's going on inside the AI that well. You can just take the AI as given and put this cryptographic thing on top of it. These AI alignment purists tend to be very skeptical that anything along those lines could possibly work, but I think at least in the near term these things might help, might give us more time, and we can make progress on them and worry about the next thing when we get to it. That is kind of what we do in science.

For a certain depth of neural networks, they show that you can insert a backdoor where if the network gets this certain bizarre input, then it does some special thing that you want it to do, such as switching itself off. Even if you could see all the weights of the neural net, it would be computationally intractable for you to find that secret input if you weren't told it. You would have to solve a hard cryptographic problem. In that case, it's something called the planted clique problem: given a large graph that looks kind of random, find some anomalously large set of vertices that are all connected to one another. That's what is known in theoretical computer science as the planted clique problem, and they could show that finding the backdoor is at least as hard as solving that.

They viewed that mostly as a negative for AI safety: a bad person could insert this backdoor into a machine learning model that people would then use, and no one would be able to detect it, and that bad person could trigger the backdoor whenever they wanted to. Like many things in science, if the world gives you a lemon, you can make lemonade. Whether something is good or bad all depends on who is doing it. This could also be seen as a positive for AI alignment. What if we use these backdoors to insert a cryptographic off switch into a powerful AI model? You could have a robot where only humans know this secret instruction that will cause the robot to shut down, and even if the robot knows its own weights and could modify them, it would not easily find that shutdown instruction. That's an idea I've been playing with.

I think we're really at the beginning of this thing. I could easily imagine this being a large part of the whole future of cryptography: what kind of cryptographic stuff can you insert into a machine learning model, or how hard is it to detect that stuff once inserted? I've taken to calling this neurocryptography. Someone else suggested calling it deep crypto, but I'm not sure; I think we have to veto that name. That's something I've been thinking about. In some sense, I think it's possible to make progress here just because you don't really have to understand what's going on inside the AI that well. You can just take the AI as given and put this cryptographic thing on top of it. These AI alignment purists tend to be very skeptical that anything along those lines could possibly work, but I think at least in the near term these things might help, might give us more time, and we can make progress on them and worry about the next thing when we get to it. That is kind of what we do in science.

items.question: Why don't you share Eliezer Yudkowsky's conclusion that further AI scaling should be shut down through an internationally enforced agreement?
items.object: Eliezer Yudkowsky's proposal to halt further AI scaling
items.answer:
I think that if you take Eliezer's starting assumptions, that at any point AI could just go off a cliff, become superintelligent, then at that point we should expect, first of all, this orthogonality thesis, which says that an arbitrarily smart AI could have, from our standpoint, arbitrarily stupid goals, like converting the whole universe into paper clips or things like that. Second, instrumental convergence, which says that no matter what the AI's goals, as a first step it's probably going to want to amass as much power and resources as possible to help it achieve its goals. We also believe in the possibility, the likelihood I should say, of deceptive alignment: an AI that will pretend to be doing all the things we want and following our instructions, but is actually just biding its time until the moment to strike against humanity. At that moment, maybe we'll all drop dead from some engineered toxin at the same second, or something like that, and we'll never have seen it coming. If you accept all of those assumptions, then I think you logically end up where he now is, saying, "Just shut it all down. It is more important than preventing nuclear war," and have an international agreement to prevent any further scaling of AI, enforced, as he explicitly said, via the threat of air strikes against anyone who didn't cooperate.

I am not at that point. I get off the train in several places. One of them is, even if one person believes there is not evidence of that now that can be made legible to the whole world, right now I think the death toll from GPT stands at zero. There was unfortunately a man in Belgium who committed suicide after spending a lot of time interacting with a language model. The causation is hard to tease out; he obviously was depressed beforehand and had some conditions. Let's say, out of hundreds of millions of people who've used these things, the death toll is either zero or one. If and when a language model is used by terrorists to help them design a terrorist attack, a new weapon, a new engineered pandemic, or something like that, and it causes mass suffering, I think at that point the whole conversation will be different. All the governments will be passing legislation to try to control this, restrict this, slow it down, and the companies themselves will want to slow it down. They may want to make money, but they also don't want to be killing people and destroying the world.

The issue is that we're not at that point. Some people think it's inevitable that it's going to get there; other people don't think so. There's one hypothesis that says these language models, as impressive as they are, are ultimately bottlenecked by how much intelligence was in their training data. They're never going to be more intelligent than the best experts that they can find on the internet to train themselves on. To the extent that people believe that thesis, maybe this never becomes that dangerous.

items.question: How do you assess the position that language models are merely stochastic parrots yet are dangerous enough to require shutting them down?
items.object: The combination of dismissing language models as stochastic parrots and demanding their shutdown
items.answer:
What I've found the hardest to wrap my head around are the people who, on the one hand, want to dismiss language models as stochastic parrots, glorified autocomplete, just not very impressive or interesting; they don't truly understand the world or semantics, they don't have symbol grounding or anything like that. But on the other hand they also think language models are terrifying and have to be shut down. That combination seems very hard to make consistent. You can make it consistent, you can reconcile those two views, but you seem to have to say something like, "The reason language models are dangerous is that most people are idiots. I can easily see that this is unimpressive and a stochastic parrot, but all the simpletons, the plebeians, will be tricked by this, and it will ruin their lives somehow."

For people who think language models are not impressive or intelligent, I think they are inadvertently making an argument that there's no reason to stop scaling. Scaling should actually be fine. We'll see that things run into a limit, as the skeptics predicted, and we'll learn something from that, and that will be that. To really have an intellectually consistent case for stopping the scaling, the consistent case I see is the existential risk case, the vaguely Yudkowsky case, that this could make a sudden sharp turn to causing a catastrophe for the world.

items.question: Why are you skeptical of a scenario in which AI suddenly destroys humanity while everything still appears to be fine?
items.object: The scenario of AI suddenly causing human extinction without preceding warning signs
items.answer: What I'm skeptical of is the scenario where everything seems fine and then instantly we all drop dead. If we've learned anything from this generation of AI, it's that it undergoes a learning process as humans undergo a learning process, not identical to our learning process. Before it's amazing at math, it's mediocre at math; before it's amazing at poetry, it's mediocre at poetry. Before it is amazing at deceiving humans and taking over the world, it would first be mediocre at those things. It would try to deceive people and not do very well, or be able to help bad humans take power in some limited way, kill some limited number of people, as opposed to destroying the entire world. I feel like we might as well worry about those risks first.
